concept.name: Equity curve
concept.definition: The time series of a trading account's or strategy's value — cumulative realized profit/loss plus open equity, net of deposits and withdrawals — plotted over time. It is the primary visual record of performance, from which drawdown, time under water, and related statistics are computed.
concept.intuition: It is the strategy's cardiogram: trend, smoothness, and depth of dips say more about robustness than any single return number.
concept.mechanics: Mark the account to market each period and plot cumulative equity; read off slope (return), path volatility, drawdowns (peak-to-trough declines), and recovery times. Some practitioners overlay a moving average on the curve and reduce size when equity falls below it ('equity curve trading').
concept.formula: E_t = E_0 + sum_{i=1..t} PnL_i (+ deposits - withdrawals); drawdown at t = (max_{s<=t} E_s - E_t) / max_{s<=t} E_s.
concept.failure_modes: A smooth equity curve can be manufactured by illiquid marks or by hiding open losses (marking only closed trades), and backtested curves embed overfitting — the live realization is one path from a distribution the backtest does not show. Curve-based size rules can whipsaw at regime boundaries.
concept.misconceptions: The equity curve is not just a price chart of profits — conventions differ on open equity and cash flows — and two curves with identical endpoints can represent radically different risk through different drawdowns and time under water.
concept.example: An account starting at $100k that reaches $130k, falls to $110k, and recovers to $140k shows a 15.4% mid-path drawdown on its equity curve — invisible if you only compare start and end values.
